headline: Barrister Gohar calls for dialogue to ease political tensions
description: PTI chairman urges serious and sincere negotiations to resolve outstanding issues
author: Web Desk
article_text:
PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan has called for dialogue to resolve political issues, warning that tensions should not be allowed to escalate further.

Speaking to the media at the Peshawar High Court on Tuesday, Gohar also criticised what he described as the government’s failure to implement a court order allowing a meeting with party founder Imran Khan at Adiala Jail.

Referring to the detention of former chief minister Sohail Afridi and the former KP Assembly speaker, Gohar welcomed the decision to refer the matter to the high court’s chief justice for the formation of a larger bench, saying court rulings should apply equally to everyone.

He said the party had sought a meeting with Imran Khan and access to medical treatment for him, but the court’s order in this regard had not been implemented.

Gohar called for an end to what he described as political victimisation and demanded the release of Imran Khan’s sisters and PTI lawmakers.

He said Imran Khan had met his lawyer, Salman Safdar, on Monday and discussed matters relating to his cases, adding that the issue could have been avoided had the meeting taken place earlier.

Criticising remarks made by PTI leader Barrister Saif, Gohar said he had not expected him to make such statements. He also questioned why PTI leaders had not been approached for comments.

Gohar reiterated that the PTI never opposed negotiations, adding that any dialogue should be held with seriousness and sincerity.

headline: Iran warns of response without 'geographical limits'
description: Military chief Maj-Gen Ali Abdollahi sets out five conditions for lasting security
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Iran’s top military commander has warned that the country’s armed forces would respond to any threat without geographical limits, while setting out five conditions Tehran considers necessary for lasting security.

Maj-General Ali Abdollahi, chief of staff of Iran’s Armed Forces and commander of the Khatam Al Anbiya Central Headquarters, said the military had the capacity to strike both the material and non-material assets of its adversaries, according to state broadcaster IRIB.

He described Iran as a “fourth centre of global power”, citing its control over the Strait of Hormuz, a key global energy route, and its ability to determine the rules governing passage through the waterway.

Abdollahi said Tehran’s conditions for lasting security included an end to wars on all fronts, particularly in Lebanon and Gaza, and a rejection of negotiations conducted under military threats.

He also called for the complete removal of sanctions against Iran, the release of its frozen assets and compensation for damage caused by wars.

He said Iran considered itself a “creditor rather than a debtor” in this regard.

The remaining conditions were recognition of Iran’s sovereignty over the Strait of Hormuz, replacing the US-led security framework with what he called a “Hormuz mechanism”, and guarantees against renewed military attacks through security arrangements led by countries in the region.

The remarks came amid continued tensions between Tehran and Washington following the war launched by the United States and Israel against Iran on February 28.

Iran has repeatedly demanded an end to the US naval blockade and the lifting of economic sanctions as part of efforts to reach a diplomatic settlement.

Separately, Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who leads Tehran’s negotiating team, said on Tuesday that Iran had delivered a “firm and rational” response to Washington, adding that the United States must now decide whether to prevent another war.

Ghalibaf warned that any renewed US military action would prompt an “unpredictable” Iranian response without geographical limits.

headline: Democrats lead in key Senate races ahead of US midterms, poll finds
description: New poll shows Democrats gaining ground in Republican-held states, including Texas and Kansas
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Democratic candidates are leading in six of seven key US Senate battlegrounds, including traditionally Republican states Texas and Kansas, according to a New York Times/Siena poll released days before the midterm elections. The race in Iowa is virtually tied.

The survey found Democrats ahead in five Republican-held states — Alaska, Kansas, Maine, Ohio and Texas while the party also holds a double-digit lead in Michigan, where the Senate seat is currently held by a Democrat.

In Texas, Democratic state lawmaker James Talarico leads Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton by 50% to 43%.

In Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton is ahead of Republican Senator Roger Marshall by 49% to 44%.

In Ohio, former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown leads Republican Senator Jon Husted by 49% to 44%, while Democrat Troy Jackson is ahead of Republican Senator Susan Collins in Maine by 51% to 45%.

In Alaska, former Democratic representative Mary Peltola leads Republican Senator Dan Sullivan by 48% to 46%.

Iowa is the closest contest, with Democrat Josh Turek leading Republican Representative Ashley Hinson by 48% to 47%.

In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El Sayed leads Republican Mike Rogers by 53% to 42%.

Don Levy, executive director of the Siena Research Institute, said the findings suggest Democrats could win control of the Senate, although several races remain within the poll’s margin of error.

The survey also found signs of dissatisfaction with Trump’s presidency and the Republican Party’s handling of the economy.

Only 38% of likely voters across the seven states approved of Trump’s job performance.

Democrats held a nine-point advantage over Republicans on which party voters trusted more to address the cost of living. Democratic candidates also led among independent voters in all seven states surveyed.

However, the poll offered some positive signs for Republicans. Voters who made their decisions within the previous month favoured Republican candidates by nine points, while several races remained too close to call.

The surveys were conducted from October 23 to November 1, with state-level margins of sampling error ranging from 3.4 percentage points in Texas to five points in Alaska.

Democrats need to gain at least four Republican-held seats to take control of the Senate.

headline: Early voting data points to Democratic advantage in midterm polls
description: Democrats lead in pre-election turnout, but election day voting could change picture
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Democrats have held a significant lead in early voting ahead of the US midterm elections, with pre-election turnout higher than in 2022 and a more diverse group of voters casting ballots, according to data tracked by CNN.

Data compiled by CNN, the Associated Press and analytics firm Catalist show that Democratic voters accounted for a larger share of early ballots than Republicans across 25 states.

Democrats led Republicans by 13 percentage points in early voting, an increase of more than three points compared with the same stage of the 2022 midterm elections, according to Catalist.

headline: PSX: KSE-100 settles above 168,000 level
description: Benchmark index gains 1,454.80 points or 0.87% during the trading session
author: Business Recorder
article_text:
The Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) witnessed a strong bullish session on Tuesday amid expectations of a positive outcome from talks between the US and Iran, with the benchmark KSE-100 Index closing above the 168,000 level.

The market opened on a positive note, with buying activity pushing the index higher during the morning session. The benchmark initially gained momentum, climbing towards its intraday high of 168,469.78 points, reflecting strong investor interest.

However, the upward momentum weakened around midday as profit-taking emerged, dragging the index lower towards its intraday low of 167,308.65 points. The market subsequently moved in a relatively narrow range, with intermittent buying and selling keeping the index under pressure.

During the final trading hours, renewed buying interest helped the benchmark recover some of its earlier losses.

At close, the benchmark index settled at 168,018.86, up 1,454.80 points or 0.87%.

Analysts were of the view that the buying interest reflects a shift in how investors are reading the geopolitical situation, not an absence of risk.

“Renewed diplomatic engagement on the Middle East conflict has pulled international oil prices lower, and for Pakistan that matters directly through the import bill, the current account and inflation,” Saad Hanif, Head of Research at Ismail Iqbal Securities, told Business Recorder.

“At the same time, the market had corrected through October, so investors who stayed on the sidelines are now selectively re-entering index heavyweights in banks, E&Ps and cement, where valuations look reasonable against earnings,” he said.

However, the recovery remains headline-driven, said Saad.

“Any breakdown in peace talks or a renewed spike in oil could reverse sentiment quickly, so we would expect volatility to persist in the near term, with investors favouring fundamentally strong, dividend-paying stocks.”

Similarly, Waqas Ghani, Head of Research at JS Global, said that the equities remain positive amid “expectations of some development on talks between the US and Iran”.

On Monday, PSX closed marginally higher as support from select heavyweights was offset by renewed selling pressure in refinery stocks following a government decision to absorb higher petrol import costs through a reduction in the Petroleum Levy. The benchmark KSE-100 Index gained 154.81 points, or 0.09%, to close at 166,564.07 points.

Globally, stocks edged lower at the start of Asian trade on Tuesday, and oil prices stabilised after the previous session’s tumble, with ‌investors on edge ahead of the start of voting for the US midterm elections.

MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan was down 0.9%, led by a decline of as much as 3.8% in Korean shares.

S&P 500 e-mini futures edged up 0.1%, while Japanese markets are closed for a holiday.

Overnight, stocks on Wall Street edged ⁠lower, with the S&P 500 slipping 0.5% as tech sector earnings weighed on investor confidence, even as data showed US manufacturing activity picked up in October amid ​strong domestic demand.

Apple shares extended losses, falling 2.8% in after-hours trading after the iPhone maker on Monday forecast lower gross margins for the crucial holiday quarter, citing rising ​memory-chip costs, and projected services revenue growth that fell well short of Wall Street expectations.

Investors are also preparing to vote in the US midterm elections, where President Donald Trump’s Republican Party is facing a challenge to keep its hold on Congress.

Opinion polls favour the Democrats to win the House, though the Senate remains too close to call. Prediction market sites Polymarket and Kalshi currently ​assign around a 75% probability that the Democrats will control the Senate.

headline: Investors ready for possible shake-up in Congress as Election Day arrives
description: Investors brace for potential volatility as Democrats seek control of Congress
author: Reuters
article_text:
Investors are weighing the market implications of a possible shift in control of the US Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections, focused on whether a strong Democratic showing could pave the way for greater volatility in ​asset prices, particularly the AI trade, which has been a main driver for markets.

The midterms come at ‌a fragile time for markets, with a swoon in AI shares causing investor unease that could be exacerbated by the election results. Tuesday’s outcome could hold broad implications for market-sensitive areas including the AI data-centre buildout, the US fiscal outlook, defence spending, and regulation in areas such as healthcare, banking and cryptocurrencies.

President ​Donald Trump’s Republican Party has controlled both chambers of Congress during the first two years of his second term. Opinion polls show the Democrats are likely to take the House, while the Senate is too close to call.

“While probabilities increasingly favour a Blue sweep, several tightly contested Senate races leave open some possibility of Republican control of ​the Senate or, conversely, a greater than expected Democratic foothold in the Senate,” Scott Chronert, US equity strategist at Citigroup, ​said in a research note. “Equity market reaction is likely positive in the former case and negative in the latter.”

Strategists at UBS Global Wealth Management have assigned a 50% probability of a Democratic sweep, a 40% chance of Democrats winning the House while Republicans retain the Senate, and ​a 10% probability that Republicans hang onto both chambers.

“The most visible effects of a change in congressional control would likely ​be greater oversight of the administration and more difficult fiscal negotiations,” Mark Haefele, chief investment officer at UBS Global Wealth Management, said ‌in a ⁠note on Monday.

A Democratic-led Congress could exert greater scrutiny over AI companies, in part due to growing public opposition to data centers, a risk for a market that has been lifted by such investment spending. While analysts doubt any viable legislation would severely undermine the data-centre buildout regardless of the election outcome, they expect a Democratic sweep to lead to investigations ​into the technology sector.

Many investors have ​said they are eager ⁠to get past the elections, which have hung over the markets for the last several weeks. Since 1970, in midterm election years, the S&P 500 index has gained in every six-month ​period following the election, according to Edward Jones.

While equity volatility has increased in recent ​sessions, option-market traders ⁠are nonetheless not bracing for a massive stock market move following the election results.

Options on the S&P 500 index are priced for a move of about 0.8% in either direction on Wednesday, slightly higher than the 0.6% average implied daily move over the ⁠past month, ​according to ORATS data.

headline: Trump's Justice Dept identifies where US election monitors will be in the 50 states
description: Justice Department calls it the largest Election Day monitoring effort in US history
author: Reuters
article_text:
The US Justice Department said on Tuesday it was deploying 1,000 election monitors and observers ​to all 50 states in what it called ‌the largest Election Day monitoring effort in history.

A Justice Department statement identified which jurisdictions within the states would receive monitors and observers.

Department ​officials have said priorities include areas with a history ​of voter access issues and places with competitive ⁠races that could be targets of voter intimidation.

The ​Trump administration has taken an increasingly aggressive approach to election oversight, ​pressing states for voter-registration data and arguing that stricter measures are needed to ensure public confidence in the vote. Critics view ​the moves as federal overreach.

The expanded federal monitoring program ​led several states to issue new guidelines to local election officials ‌and ⁠poll workers about the limited authority DOJ observers will have on Election Day.

“Election monitors will be checking for compliance with the federal voting rights statutes that fall ​within the jurisdiction ​of the (Civil ⁠Rights Division),” the Justice Department statement said.

Some state and local laws allow election officials to ​prevent DOJ monitors from being present inside ​polling ⁠locations. DOJ staff cannot conduct investigations on the spot or otherwise stop anyone from voting.

The number of monitors is ⁠roughly ​triple the number in the last ​midterm election. The deployment would be the largest observation effort in ​the department’s history.

headline: Security forces kills 17 militants in two operations in Balochistan: ISPR
description: Pakistan Army soldier martyred during exchange of fire
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Security forces killed 17 militants in two separate intelligence-based operations in Pakistan’s southwestern Balochistan province, while a Pakistan Army soldier was also martyred during an exchange of fire, ISPR said on Tuesday.

According to the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the operations were conducted on November 1 in Kachhi and Kharan districts following intelligence reports about the presence of militants affiliated with what it described as Indian-backed proxy groups.

In the first operation, security forces targeted militants in the Sanni area of Kachhi district after they attempted to establish a blockade. The attempt was thwarted, and 10 militants were killed, with weapons and ammunition recovered from their possession, the ISPR said.

In a separate operation in Kharan district, security forces identified and destroyed a militant hideout. Seven militants were killed during an intense exchange of fire, while weapons and ammunition were also recovered, according to the statement.

A Pakistan Army soldier, Sepoy Hikmatullah, was killed during the operation in Kharan. He was 25 years old and belonged to Karak district, the military said.

The ISPR said clearance operations were underway in both areas to eliminate any remaining militants.

It added that counterterrorism operations would continue under the Azm-e-Istehkam framework, approved by the Federal Apex Committee under the National Action Plan, until terrorism and its alleged foreign support were eliminated.

headline: Petroleum minister promises relief to LPG consumers through market reforms
description: Government abolishes quota-based distribution and establishes funds to support vulnerable households
author: APP
article_text:
Pakistan is introducing a series of reforms to open the liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) sector to competition, curb monopolistic practices and bring down prices, Federal Minister for Petroleum Ali Pervaiz Malik said on Tuesday.

Addressing a press conference alongside Federal Minister for Information and Broadcasting Attaullah Tarar, Malik said the government had decided to abolish the existing quota-based distribution mechanism and introduce transparent auctions to encourage competition and ensure affordable fuel for consumers.

Tarar said Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had directed the introduction of a merit-based and transparent system in the LPG sector by ending monopolistic practices and abolishing the long-standing discretionary quota system.

He termed the initiative a historic step, saying no previous government had attempted to dismantle the monopoly of a few individuals and introduce a competitive mechanism based on merit.

Malik said the government aimed to ensure the availability of natural gas through pipeline networks wherever possible, while providing LPG at affordable prices to households not connected to the gas network.

Explaining the international pricing mechanism, Malik said Saudi Aramco’s monthly Contract Price (CP), based on propane and butane, served as an international benchmark for LPG, similar to Platts for petroleum products.

He said the Saudi Aramco CP had increased from $540 per tonne in March to $756 per tonne, prompting the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (OGRA) to revise domestic prices accordingly.

Pakistan currently meets around 70 per cent of its LPG requirements through imports, while domestic production stands at approximately 2,200 to 2,500 tonnes per day, he said.

Malik said the existing free-on-board (FOB) pricing mechanism did not adequately account for import-related costs, encouraging the growth of informal and grey-market channels.

The government had therefore decided to introduce competition and encourage public and private companies to import LPG from international markets at competitive prices, he added.

Pakistan State Oil (PSO), Sui Southern Gas Company and Pakistan LNG Limited, along with other state-owned entities, had been directed to arrange bulk LPG supplies through government-to-government and business-to-business arrangements, the minister said.

These companies would publicly disclose monthly cost components, including Saudi Aramco’s CP, premiums, freight charges and other expenses, on their websites to ensure transparency.

Private-sector companies would also be encouraged to import LPG, while increased competition and supply were expected to help bring prices down, he said.

Referring to prevailing international market conditions, Malik said LPG was trading at a premium of $300 to $400 per tonne over the Saudi Aramco CP.

Taking all costs into account, the prevailing spot-market price was estimated at Rs450 to Rs500 per kilogram, he said, adding that the government would publicly disclose relevant pricing details and welcome any importer capable of bringing the product at a lower price.

Announcing the end of the existing quota-based distribution mechanism, Malik said domestic LPG production would instead be auctioned in transparent lots of five to 10 tonnes among OGRA-licensed companies.

Auction results would be made public, with the process monitored by the Petroleum Secretary and OGRA chairman, he added.

To protect consumers in remote and hard areas, the government would ensure proper utilisation of the 10 per cent LPG quota allocated under the policy, Malik said.

State-owned companies would procure this quota directly from producers and distribute it fairly among designated districts in consultation with provincial chief secretaries.

Additional revenue generated through the auction mechanism would be channelled into a price stabilisation fund and a vulnerable consumers’ protection fund, he said.

The funds would help provide LPG at subsidised rates to deserving consumers identified under criteria to be developed in consultation with the Benazir Income Support Programme and provincial governments.

Malik said the Competition Commission had also been asked to take measures against cartelisation and anti-competitive practices, while OGRA would strengthen its licensing and audit mechanisms to prevent hoarding and profiteering.

The National Explosives Department would oversee safety standards, including the quality and testing of LPG cylinders and transportation bowsers, he added.

Tarar said the government was also taking measures to protect consumers from the impact of the global energy crisis, adding that the prime minister had initially provided subsidies worth Rs133 billion to prevent increases in petrol and diesel prices and ensure fuel availability.

Subsequently, a targeted subsidy mechanism was introduced through the Fuel Relief Scheme to extend assistance to deserving and underprivileged segments of society, he said.

He added that OGRA had started publishing all relevant details on its website as part of the government’s efforts to improve transparency and strengthen regulatory oversight.

The new LPG arrangements were expected to become fully operational before winter, Malik said.

He added that the current crisis should also serve as an opportunity to strengthen Pakistan’s energy infrastructure, develop storage and import facilities and make the country more resilient to future supply disruptions.

The ultimate objective was to establish a transparent and competitive LPG market that ensured affordable fuel, improved consumer services and protection for the most vulnerable sections of society, Malik said.

According to a press release issued by the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (OGRA) on Tuesday, the regulator revised the ex-depot prices of petroleum products under the federal government’s petroleum pricing mechanism.

OGRA said the price adjustments were necessitated by global developments, including changes in Platts rates, premiums and incidentals.

On Monday, the government reduced the price of diesel by Rs7.76 per litre to Rs395.20 and petrol by Rs3.40 per litre to Rs374.51 per litre.

headline: Pakistan successfully conducts flight test of Fa’az missile
description: Senior military officers and scientists witness test of the country's first indigenous air-to-air missile
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Pakistan has successfully conducted the flight test of its first indigenously developed Fa’az air-to-air missile, marking a milestone in the country’s aerospace and defence capabilities, the military’s media wing said.

The missile is equipped with a terminal guidance system and is capable of engaging enemy aerial targets at extended ranges, according to a news release issued by Inter Services Public Relations (ISPR).

The Fa’az missile is expected to enhance the operational flexibility of the Pakistan Air Force and strengthen the country’s overall defence posture, ISPR said.

The successful flight test reflects the technical maturity, innovation and self-reliance of Pakistan’s defence industry, the statement added.

The launch was witnessed by senior officers of the Pakistan Armed Forces, along with scientists and engineers involved in the development of the weapon system.

The president, prime minister, chief of army staff and chief of defence forces, and services chiefs congratulated the scientists and engineers on the achievement, the statement said.

headline: US midterm elections begin with control of Congress at stake
description: Democrats seek to wrest control of at least one chamber from Republicans
author: Web Desk | Reuters
article_text:
Americans headed to the polls in Tuesday’s midterm elections to deliver a verdict on the first two years of President Donald Trump’s second term, with surveys and nonpartisan analysts favouring Democrats to wrest the House of Representatives from Republicans while control of ​the Senate remains uncertain.

The nationwide vote will decide all 435 seats in the House of Representatives, 35 Senate seats and governorships in 36 states.

State legislative positions and local offices are also up for election, alongside policy referendums in some states, according to Anadolu news agency.

The first polling stations opened at 6am local time in New York, Connecticut, New Jersey, Virginia and parts of Indiana and Kentucky, with voting getting underway at staggered times across the country.

Republicans currently hold majorities in both the House and Senate, but Democrats are aiming to capture at least one chamber, potentially limiting Trump’s ability to advance his legislative priorities.

Polls will close at different times across the country’s time zones, with the first regular closures scheduled for 6pm Eastern Time.

headline: Seen and heard at the US midterm elections
description: Voters in Brooklyn, Atlanta, Austin and Miami cite the cost of living, immigration, Iran and fears of socialism as Democrats eye a House majority
author: AFP
article_text:
AFP has deployed reporters, photographers and video journalists across the United States as American voters head to the polls for crucial midterm elections.

Here is a round-up of interviews on Tuesday at polling stations where voters agreed to share their thoughts about what was on their minds and what motivated their choices.

Hopeful Democrats

With polling data suggesting the Democratic Party is on track to capture a majority in the House of Representatives and perhaps even in the Senate, many left-leaning voters said they were hopeful about the results.

“Two years ago was a really devastating outcome for me,” Emma Mondadori, a 39-year-old who works in philanthropy, told AFP in Brooklyn, New York, referring to President Donald Trump’s election.

“I’ve been really looking forward to this day where we get to have a say again in the future of our country… I’m cautiously hopeful, optimistic.”

The cost of living

With gasoline prices up by a third since last year and diesel nearly double — not to mention sharp food price inflation — everyday spending was on many people’s minds.

“It’s about the cost of living, gas prices, those kinds of things. It needs to change for the everyday person, and I’m an everyday person,” Donta Comer, a 38-year-old project manager in Atlanta, Georgia, told AFP.

Tom, a 27-year-old businessman at the same polling station who declined to give his surname, agreed.

“Everyone, at least in my generation, is a little frustrated with the affordability crisis and gas prices and what’s going on abroad,” added the non-partisan voter.

Leadership referendum

Mid-term elections are typically seen as a form of referendum on the sitting president.

And few leaders have polarised public opinion as strongly as Donald Trump.

“I’m independent, but I voted Democrat; I just wanted to go back into the culture of decency, integrity, honesty, and the rest follows,” Yan Cardineau, 59, told AFP in Austin, Texas. “If we lose that, it doesn’t matter how much money you make.”

Estrella Roque, a 69-year-old voter of Cuban origin, told AFP in Miami she had voted Republican.

“What I like about the Republicans is that they can fix the country,” she explained in Spanish. “Donald Trump hasn’t been given time to show who he really is.”

Immigration

In his final pitch to voters, Trump has stressed his success in reducing immigration and stopping crossings along the southern border with Mexico.

While his tough stance plays well with his core supporters, others have been put off by the brutal tactics used by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents.

“I am very concerned about climate change, school violence and the situation with people who still don’t have immigration status in this country,” Diana Alvarez, a 38-year-old Cuban-born attorney, said in Doral, Florida.

“It’s tough for any presidency, but this one in particular has been a little violent and aggressive (with migrants), and I don’t think that was necessary.”

Iran

Trump’s most consequential foreign policy decision of his second term — the February 28 attack on Iran along with Israel — was referenced by several voters.

“It’s discouraging. Again, promises made, promises not kept. ‘No new wars’ was the mantra,” Wes Pyron, a 37-year-old who works at an environmental health nonprofit in Washington, said.

“I don’t understand what we’re doing there; objectives aren’t clear, priorities aren’t clear.”

Fears of socialism

Many Republican candidates and Trump have sought to portray their Democratic rivals as dangerous tax-and-spend Socialists intent on destroying American capitalism.

“A lot of today’s younger people think socialism is the way to go,” Daryl Ruley, an 84-year-old in Austin, Texas, told AFP. “They don’t understand history if they believe that’s the case.”

Maru Restrepo, a 70-year-old voter of Colombian origin in Miami, said Democrats had become “very Socialist, Communist, and Muslim.”

Michigan

In one of the most widely watched races for the Senate — in Michigan — Democrat candidate Abdul El-Sayed has made free universal healthcare and ending US support for Israel key planks of his platform.

The Muslim former medical administrator has been called a ‘jihadist’ by Trump and has been smeared with accusations of sympathising with groups such as the Muslim Brotherhood or Hamas.

“We just got to get it done because we all need help. I need help,” said Makeyla Borndes, a 51-year-old former teacher who was forced to retire after falling down a staircase.

She wore several El-Sayed pins on her green apron and neon pink socks.

headline: US midterms: the races to watch
description: Democrats need a net gain of four Senate seats and 218 in the House, but polling errors, redrawn districts and record spending cloud the outcome
author: AFP
article_text:
Americans voted on Tuesday in midterm elections to decide whether President Donald Trump’s Republicans retain control of Congress or spend the final two years of his term confronting Democratic majorities.

High living costs, the war with Iran and Trump’s poor approval ratings have helped Democrats expand the electoral map, with unusually tight contests even in Republican strongholds.

But polling errors, redrawn districts and record campaign spending make the outcome uncertain.

The arithmetic

Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take the upper chamber of Congress, as a 50-50 tie would leave Republicans in charge through Vice President JD Vance’s tie-breaking vote.

All 435 seats in the House of Representatives are contested. It currently has 218 Republicans and one Republican-aligned independent, 214 Democrats, and two vacancies.

Democrats need at least 218 seats in the lower chamber to clinch a majority in the new session.

Senate: eight battlegrounds

North Carolina: The state’s Democratic ex-governor Roy Cooper faces Republican operative Michael Whatley in a bid to flip the seat being vacated by retiring Senator Thom Tillis, a vocal Republican Trump critic.

Strong polling for Cooper prompted both parties to shift some spending elsewhere, but the outcome is key for Democrats.

Texas: Democrat James Talarico, a Christian progressive, faces Trump-backed state Attorney General Ken Paxton, whose controversies have helped turn a longtime Republican stronghold into a closely watched contest. Paxton retains a loyal conservative following and enormous outside financial support.

Ohio: Former Democratic senator Sherrod Brown seeks a comeback against Republican Jon Husted, who was appointed to replace Vance when he became vice president. Among the country’s most expensive races, it’s also a test of whether economic discontent can shift a state that has moved sharply rightward.

Maine: Republican Susan Collins faces former state Senate leader Troy Jackson. She has repeatedly survived difficult elections in a state that votes Democratic for president.

Alaska: Former Democratic congresswoman Mary Peltola challenges Republican Daniel Sullivan. Her strong standing among voters has made another Trump-voting state unexpectedly competitive.

Iowa: Republican congresswoman Ashley Hinson and Democrat Josh Turek compete for retiring Republican Senator Joni Ernst’s seat, while soaring agricultural and energy costs are prominent issues.

Kansas: Democratic pastor Adam Hamilton is challenging Republican Roger Marshall in a state that ’t elected a Democratic senator since 1932. Tight polling has prompted Trump to campaign for Marshall.

Michigan: An important Republican pickup opportunity pits former congressman Mike Rogers against progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed to fill the seat of retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters.

House: watch the suburbs

New York’s 17th district: Republican Mike Lawler faces Democrat Cait Conley in a Hudson Valley seat won by Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election.

Nebraska’s 2nd: Republican Don Bacon’s retirement leaves a competitive Omaha-area seat contested by Republican Brinker Harding and Democrat Denise Powell.

Pennsylvania: Republican incumbents Ryan Mackenzie, Rob Bresnahan and Scott Perry face closely watched Democratic challenges. Nearby, New Jersey’s 7th district, where Rebecca Bennett challenges Republican Tom Kean Jr, is also in play.

Virginia’s 2nd: Democrat Elaine Luria seeks to reclaim the coastal seat she lost to Republican Jennifer Kiggans in 2022.

Iowa: Three Republican-held districts in the state’s east and centre could provide an early indication of whether Democrats are making broad gains.

Signs of a wave?

For an indication of the scale of any Democratic advance, watch two Republican-held House districts in Virginia: the 1st, where Shannon Taylor challenges Robert Wittman, and the 5th, where former congressman Tom Perriello wants to unseat John McGuire.

A Democratic gain in Kentucky’s Republican-leaning 6th district, or unexpected defeats for Republicans in Florida’s 13th and Wisconsin’s 1st, would likewise signal a particularly broad electoral swing.

Conversely, Democrats face dangers of their own in redrawn districts, including Alabama’s 2nd, where Shomari Figures is defending his seat, and Texas’s 34th, where Vicente Gonzalez faces Republican Eric Flores.

headline: US vote seen as referendum on Trump presidency
description: Polls point to a Democratic House majority and possibly the Senate, as voter anger over prices, Iran and Trump’s ratings drives turnout
author: AFP
article_text:
Americans voted on Tuesday in a midterm election seen as a nationwide referendum on Donald Trump that could wrest control of Congress from his Republican Party and impose major restraints on the remaining two years of his presidency.

Polls predict the Democrats will win a majority in the House of Representatives and possibly seize the Senate on the back of voter resentment at an unpopular president, soaring energy costs and the ongoing conflict with Iran.

Republicans losing the House would give Democrats the power to stall the 80-year-old Trump’s legislative agenda and launch sweeping investigations of his administration.

A Senate defeat would threaten his ability to appoint Supreme Court justices and senior officials.

“It’s just about the cost of living, gas prices, those kinds of things,” Donta Comer, a 38-year-old project manager voting in an Atlanta suburb, told AFP. “It needs to change for the everyday person, and I’m an everyday person.”

Trump defended his record in a final TV phone-in pitch to voters on Tuesday, saying he had rebuilt the country through his immigration crackdown, war on Iran and tariff policies.

“We have to keep America great. We’re great now. We were terrible two years ago,” Trump told “Fox & Friends.”

All 435 House seats and 35 of the 100 Senate seats are at stake, along with governorships in 36 states. Democrats need only three House gains and a net four seats in the Senate to wrest both chambers from Republican hands.

Trump returned to office promising to bring down prices, but inflation, tariffs and fuel costs inflated by the Middle East conflict have squeezed Americans.

Economic discontent

Republicans insist that Trump’s tax cuts and anti-migrant stance will benefit voters, and they are portraying Democratic candidates as left-wing radical socialists — a message that seemed to resonate with Daryl Ruley, an 84-year-old voter in Austin, Texas.

“A lot of today’s younger people think socialism is the way to go,” Ruley told AFP. “They don’t understand history if they believe that’s the case.”

But in his final public campaign appearance on Monday, Trump barely touched on the election and gave a rambling talk about his problem-plagued renovation of Washington’s Reflecting Pool.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer branded it a “pathetic closing message.”

Republicans currently hold a 53-47 Senate majority, but the battlefield has extended into once reliably conservative states like Kansas, Texas, Iowa, Ohio and Alaska.

Democrats must also defend competitive seats, including in Michigan, where a bitter internal dispute saw Congresswoman Haley Stevens endorse Republican Mike Rogers rather than the Democratic nominee, Abdul El-Sayed.

Decision Desk HQ’s final forecast projected 241 House seats for Democrats against 194 for Republicans, and a narrower 52-48 Democratic Senate majority.

Disputed results?

More than 57 million Americans had already voted early before Tuesday, indicating high engagement.

The campaign has attracted more than $11 billion in political advertising, and mega-rich Trump ally Elon Musk has poured hundreds of millions of dollars into Republican efforts.

As soon as polls close, concerns will mount over whether results will be accepted by the Republicans.

Trump, who tried to overturn his 2020 presidential election defeat, has repeatedly alleged widespread voter fraud and accused Democrats — with no evidence — of cheating.

The Justice Department, run by a close Trump ally, has already sued to potentially block certification of Alaska’s Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan narrowly loses, although a court ruled against the effort.

And the Supreme Court rejected on Monday an emergency bid to force California to set aside the mail-in ballots of more than 20,000 people on the grounds they may not be American citizens.

Trump, who will watch the midterms results at the White House on Tuesday night, signaled that if he does lose control of Congress he has a plan to defy Democrats.

“I veto everything,” he said.

headline: Trump approval near career low, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
description: Trump job approval stands at 32%, near record low; Voters favour Democrats by 46% to 38% on generic congressional ballot
author: Reuters
article_text:
President Donald Trump’s approval ​rating held near a career low as a broad swath of the US electorate saw ‌their vote in Tuesday’s congressional midterm elections as a way to oppose the Republican president, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday.

The poll results underscore Republican vulnerabilities brought on by a surge in fuel prices since Trump launched a war on ​Iran in February. Voters in the nationwide poll said they preferred Democrats over Republicans — 46% to ​38% — in what is known as a “generic ballot” question.

Still, that 8-percentage-point Democratic advantage was ⁠narrower than in a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted a week earlier, when Democrats led by 11 points.

The generic ballot ​question gives an overall view of which party voters nationwide would like to see in charge in Congress, ​though it does not capture the nuances of the state-by-state and district-by-district contests that determine control of the US Senate and US House of Representatives.

Trump’s fellow Republicans are fighting to retain the party’s majorities in Congress.

Political strategists from both parties think Democrats ​have the best shot at winning control of the House, where all 435 seats are up for grabs. ​Democrats face a more difficult path to victory in the US Senate, with the party on the defensive in Alaska ‌and Michigan ⁠in recent days.

While Trump won’t be on the ballot, he looms large in the election.

Some 32% of poll respondents said they approved of the job Trump was doing in the White House, unchanged from a week earlier and just above his record-low reading of 31% two weeks ago.

Among registered voters, some 50% of independents said ​they saw their vote in ​congressional elections as a ⁠vote against Trump, compared with 13% who said it was a vote for Trump and 33% who said the president wasn’t a factor in their vote.

Some 78% ​of voters said the rising cost of living would be very important or the ​most important ⁠issue in deciding how to vote. Asked which party was better on the issue, voters in the poll picked Democrats over Republicans, 43% to 32%.

Democrats appear to have more enthusiasm about voting, which the party hopes will lead ⁠to an ​advantage in voter turnout. Some 49% of Democratic voters said they ​are “very enthusiastic” about voting this year, compared with 33% of Republicans.

The latest Reuters/Ipsos poll surveyed 1,765 US adults online and had a ​margin of error of 2 percentage points.

headline: Ballot machine glitch hits New York county in tight House race
description: Officials insist all ballots will be counted as right-wing influencers allege fraud without evidence over Westchester County scanner problem
author: AFP
article_text:
Ballot machines malfunctioned in a hotly contested House race in New York state on Tuesday, prompting right-wing influencers to fling unfounded allegations of US midterms voter fraud even as local election officials insisted all ballots would be counted.

President Donald Trump and his allies have previously spread unproven claims about voting machines, alleging that they are faulty or unreliable.

The Westchester County Board of Elections said it was aware of an issue involving paper ballots that is preventing voting machines from accepting ballots at polling locations throughout the county.

The board “wants to reassure every voter that your vote matters, your ballot will be secure and your vote will be counted,” with ballots instead placed in emergency bags, it said in a statement.

Parts of Westchester County are included in New York’s 17th district, where incumbent Republican Mike Lawler faces Democrat Cait Conley in a House of Representatives seat that voted for Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election.

Pro-Donald Trump influencers pounced on the glitch by claiming, without evidence, that Democrats were trying to “steal” the election.

They included conspiracy theorist Laura Loomer, conservative activist Scott Pressler, and Katie Miller, a podcaster married to White House advisor Stephen Miller.

The New York State Board of Elections said on X that there has been no disruption to voting.

“Long-established emergency ballot procedures have been implemented, where completed ballots are secured, under bipartisan control, and will be counted,” it said.

The Board added in a later statement that the technical error was linked to voting machines being unable to read and accept the ballots.

“Importantly, the affected scanners rejected ballots they could not properly recognise rather than incorrectly tabulating them,” it said.

headline: 'Our presence makes a big difference': Georgia volunteers watch the polls
description: Hundreds of ACLU-organised observers are stationed at Georgia polling sites to watch for intimidation and long lines, more than double the 2024 number
author: AFP
article_text:
Linda Jones has set up a folding chair near a polling station in Atlanta, Georgia, to watch out for anything that might keep people from casting their ballots in the US midterms.

“I want to help people navigate the voting, which has gotten more and more complicated,” said the septuagenarian, who is serving as an election observer for the first time.

She and two other volunteers will keep a close watch on activity around this polling station, set up in a public library, and report any issues that arise.

“In a climate like we are in the country, there’s misinformation, there [are] actions that are taken that discourage some people from voting, certain parts of the population,” she told AFP.

The polling station where she is stationed is in Fulton County, the most populous county in the state of Georgia, where Black residents are the largest racial group.

During the 2020 presidential election, won by Democrat Joe Biden, the county became the focal point of baseless allegations of electoral fraud made by President Donald Trump.

A surge in volunteers

Rachel Glover, associate director of the election observation program at the local chapter of the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), said the volunteers play a crucial role in ensuring election integrity — from making sure no electioneering takes place near polling stations, to watching for voter intimidation, to noting long lines and ensuring accessible entrances are clearly marked.

Most of all, “it’s making sure that no one walks away from the polling location and wasn’t able to vote if they’re an eligible registered voter,” Glover said.

Some 500 election observers have been deployed by the ACLU in Georgia. About a dozen other organisations are collaborating on the operation.

Glover said the number of volunteers more than doubled compared with the 2024 presidential election won by Trump.

“We have students, older retired people, normal average working professionals who are just taking a day off to do this,” she said, all with the shared goal of “trying to fight back these attempts to silence them.”

Trump’s administration has sought to insert itself into the voting process in several ways, from trying to curb mail-in ballots to changing the rules for voter registration.

During the early voting period, Glover reported no major malfunctions, nor any sign of the immigration enforcement operations that some had feared.

Fear

Retired oncology nurse Rosa Rivera-Ayala, part of the “Vote Safe” initiative, has stationed herself near a polling place in DeKalb County, which has a majority-Black population and a large number of naturalised American citizens.

“We see things daily that just put fear in the hearts of Americans,” she told AFP. “Even people who have papers and are allowed to vote are afraid to come out for fear of being targeted.”

Rivera-Ayala is there, she said, because “our presence makes a big difference. The citizens who come to vote, I think, feel better knowing that there are poll watchers who are making sure that nothing happens to them.”

The Atlanta-based Carter Centre — founded by former Democratic president Jimmy Carter and an expert in international election observation — has been working in Georgia since 2020 to address a trust deficit in the electoral process.

For this election, it is focused on the collection and tabulation of results.

“It’s not exciting. It shouldn’t be exciting,” said Jonathan Stonestreet, who leads the effort. But the goal is to ensure “everyone can have confidence that these are the real results,” he said.

headline: Abdul El-Sayed’s Michigan Senate race could make US history
description: Progressive Democrat faces Republican Mike Rogers in a closely watched contest that could see the first Muslim elected to the US Senate
author: Web Desk
article_text:
The US Senate race in Michigan has drawn national and international attention, with Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed facing Republican Mike Rogers in a contest that could make El-Sayed the first Muslim senator in American history.

The 42-year-old El-Sayed, a physician and progressive politician, is challenging 63-year-old Rogers, a former congressman and FBI agent, for the seat being vacated by retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters.

The contest has emerged as a major political battleground in Michigan, a key swing state where Democrats and Republicans have traditionally faced close electoral competition.

El-Sayed’s campaign has attracted particular attention because of his Muslim identity and progressive policy positions. He has faced criticism from Republicans and President Donald Trump over his religious background, as well as his views on Israel, Gaza and US foreign policy.

Progressive Democrat gains momentum

El-Sayed, whose father is an Egyptian immigrant, is a Michigan-born physician who has worked with American institutions and international academic centres. He is widely regarded as part of the progressive wing of the Democratic Party.

In August 2026, he won the Democratic Senate primary, becoming the party’s first Muslim nominee for the US Senate.

His primary victory was significant given that his rival, Haley Stevens, had received backing from several influential Democratic leaders. El-Sayed, meanwhile, secured support from prominent progressive politicians, including Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

His campaign has centred on progressive policies, including calls to end US military aid to Israel.

These positions have drawn criticism from some Jewish Democrats and pro-Israel groups, which have accused him of antisemitism. El-Sayed has rejected the allegations.

Religious identity and foreign policy in focus

El-Sayed’s Muslim identity has remained a prominent issue throughout the campaign, with opponents repeatedly targeting his religious background and political positions.

His stance on Israel and the Gaza conflict has also become a major point of contention, particularly his support for ending American military assistance to Israel.

The race has consequently become a closely watched contest over religious representation and the direction of the Democratic Party’s foreign policy.

No Muslim has ever been elected to the US Senate, making El-Sayed’s candidacy particularly significant for Muslim representation in American politics.

Unexpected setback in final campaign stretch

El-Sayed faced an unexpected political setback in the final phase of the campaign when Stevens, his rival in the Democratic primary, announced her support for Republican candidate Rogers.

Rogers, a former US congressman and FBI agent, has previously contested a Senate election in Michigan. His campaign represents a potential Republican pickup opportunity in a state that has remained competitive between the two major parties.

Despite the setback, El-Sayed had maintained a strong position in several pre-election polls.

Election analysis firm Decision Desk HQ gave him a 75% chance of winning the race, while other surveys had also shown him with a narrow or substantial lead.

The outcome could have implications beyond Michigan, potentially reshaping the Senate’s political balance while marking a historic milestone for Muslim representation in the United States.

If El-Sayed defeats Rogers, he will become the first Muslim elected to the US Senate.

headline: Polls begin closing in midterms set to roil Trump presidency
description: Democrats poised to seize the House and possibly the Senate, threatening to curtail Trump’s power for the rest of his presidency
author: AFP
article_text:
Polls began closing on Tuesday in the US midterms, with Democrats poised to seize the House and potentially the Senate, threatening to shatter Donald Trump’s grip on Washington and curtail his power for the rest of his presidency.

Republicans losing the House would give Democrats the power to stall Trump’s legislative agenda and launch sweeping investigations of his administration. A Senate defeat would also threaten his ability to appoint Supreme Court justices and senior officials.

The election amounts to a nationwide judgment on Trump at a time when the mood is turning sharply against Republicans over soaring living costs and the war against Iran.

All 435 House seats and 35 of the 100 Senate seats were at stake, along with governorships in 36 states. Democrats need only three House gains and a net four seats in the Senate to wrest both chambers from Republican hands.

As the first polls began closing in Kentucky and Indiana, House Democratic Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries told reporters in Washington that the country was “on the brink of a dramatic change of direction.”

“We’re on the brink of Democrats taking back control of the House of Representatives,” he predicted.

Trump returned to office last year promising to bring down prices, but inflation, tariffs and fuel costs inflated by the Middle East conflict that he launched have squeezed Americans.

The 80-year-old’s approval rating has hovered near the low 30s, making him one of the most unpopular presidents in history.

Taylor Cook, a Los Angeles voter, told AFP that affordability and reining in the Trump administration were the two biggest election issues.

“Rent, groceries, utility bills, and property taxes keep climbing, and I want people in Congress who will actually do something about costs,” the 24-year-old said.

Economic discontent

Trump defended his record in a final TV phone-in pitch to voters on Tuesday, saying he had rebuilt the country through his immigration crackdown, war on Iran and tariffs.

“We have to keep America great. We’re great now. We were terrible two years ago,” Trump told “Fox & Friends.”

Republicans insist that Trump’s tax cuts and anti-migrant stance will benefit voters, and they have portrayed Democratic candidates as left-wing radicals — a message that has seemed to resonate with some voters.

“Democrats used to be decent in the past, but they became very socialist,” Maru Restrepo, a 70-year-old voter of Colombian origin, told AFP in Miami.

Trump has campaigned to help Republicans, but polls show he may have weighed them down instead.

In his final public appearance on Monday, Trump barely touched on the election and gave a rambling talk about his problem-plagued renovation of Washington’s Reflecting Pool.

“He’s done everything that was needed. Republicans are in a better spot now than they were four weeks ago,” a White House official told AFP.

But Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer branded Trump’s final speech “pathetic.”

Disputed results?

The Senate is a steep hill for Democrats to climb.

While Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority, the angry mood had extended the battlefield into once reliably conservative states like Kansas, Texas, Iowa, Ohio and Alaska.

But Democrats must defend competitive seats, including in Michigan, where a bitter internal dispute saw Congresswoman Haley Stevens endorse Republican Mike Rogers rather than the Democratic nominee, Abdul El-Sayed.

Decision Desk HQ’s final forecast projected 241 House seats for Democrats against 194 for Republicans, and a narrower 52-48 Democratic Senate majority.

The campaign has attracted more than $11 billion in political advertising, and mega-rich Trump ally Elon Musk has poured nearly half a billion dollars into Republican efforts.

Concerns were high that Republicans — especially Trump — would refuse to accept results if they lose.

Trump, who tried to overturn his 2020 presidential election defeat, has repeatedly alleged widespread voter fraud and accused Democrats — with no evidence — of cheating.

Voting machines malfunctioned in a hotly contested House race in New York state on Tuesday, prompting right-wing influencers to fling unfounded allegations of fraud even as local election officials insisted all ballots would be counted.

Polls began closing on Tuesday in the US midterms, with Democrats poised to seize the House and potentially the Senate, threatening to shatter Donald Trump’s grip on Washington and curtail his power for the rest of his presidency.

Republicans losing the House would give Democrats the power to stall Trump’s legislative agenda and launch sweeping investigations of his administration. A Senate defeat would also threaten his ability to appoint Supreme Court justices and senior officials.

The election amounts to a nationwide judgment on Trump at a time when the mood is turning sharply against Republicans over soaring living costs and the war against Iran.

All 435 House seats and 35 of the 100 Senate seats were at stake, along with governorships in 36 states. Democrats need only three House gains and a net four seats in the Senate to wrest both chambers from Republican hands.

As the first polls began closing in Kentucky and Indiana, House Democratic Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries told reporters in Washington that the country was “on the brink of a dramatic change of direction.”

“We’re on the brink of Democrats taking back control of the House of Representatives,” he predicted.

Trump returned to office last year promising to bring down prices, but inflation, tariffs and fuel costs inflated by the Middle East conflict that he launched have squeezed Americans.

The 80-year-old’s approval rating has hovered near the low 30s, making him one of the most unpopular presidents in history.

Taylor Cook, a Los Angeles voter, told AFP that affordability and reining in the Trump administration were the two biggest election issues.

“Rent, groceries, utility bills, and property taxes keep climbing, and I want people in Congress who will actually do something about costs,” the 24-year-old said.

Economic discontent

Trump defended his record in a final TV phone-in pitch to voters on Tuesday, saying he had rebuilt the country through his immigration crackdown, war on Iran and tariffs.

“We have to keep America great. We’re great now. We were terrible two years ago,” Trump told “Fox & Friends.”

Republicans insist that Trump’s tax cuts and anti-migrant stance will benefit voters, and they have portrayed Democratic candidates as left-wing radicals — a message that has seemed to resonate with some voters.

“Democrats used to be decent in the past, but they became very socialist,” Maru Restrepo, a 70-year-old voter of Colombian origin, told AFP in Miami.

Trump has campaigned to help Republicans, but polls show he may have weighed them down instead.

In his final public appearance on Monday, Trump barely touched on the election and gave a rambling talk about his problem-plagued renovation of Washington’s Reflecting Pool.

“He’s done everything that was needed. Republicans are in a better spot now than they were four weeks ago,” a White House official told AFP.

But Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer branded Trump’s final speech “pathetic.”

Disputed results?

The Senate is a steep hill for Democrats to climb.

While Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority, the angry mood had extended the battlefield into once reliably conservative states like Kansas, Texas, Iowa, Ohio and Alaska.

But Democrats must defend competitive seats, including in Michigan, where a bitter internal dispute saw Congresswoman Haley Stevens endorse Republican Mike Rogers rather than the Democratic nominee, Abdul El-Sayed.

Decision Desk HQ’s final forecast projected 241 House seats for Democrats against 194 for Republicans, and a narrower 52-48 Democratic Senate majority.

The campaign has attracted more than $11 billion in political advertising, and mega-rich Trump ally Elon Musk has poured nearly half a billion dollars into Republican efforts.

Concerns were high that Republicans — especially Trump — would refuse to accept results if they lose.

Trump, who tried to overturn his 2020 presidential election defeat, has repeatedly alleged widespread voter fraud and accused Democrats — with no evidence — of cheating.

Voting machines malfunctioned in a hotly contested House race in New York state on Tuesday, prompting right-wing influencers to fling unfounded allegations of fraud even as local election officials insisted all ballots would be counted.

headline: Alaskan in tight Senate race accuses Dems of 'election cheating'
description: Republican Dan Sullivan says a ‘decoy’ candidate with his name is siphoning votes, as polls show him essentially tied with Democrat Mary Peltola
author: AFP
article_text:
Hours before polls closed Tuesday in US midterm elections, Alaska Republican Senator Dan Sullivan denounced what he called “election cheating” by Democrats, highlighting a scandal that has rocked the 49th state’s midterm campaign.

Sullivan has accused the campaign apparatus of his Democratic rival Mary Peltola of recruiting a man with the same name as the Republican lawmaker to be a “decoy” candidate.

Despite the uproar, retired schoolteacher Daniel J. Sullivan’s name has remained on ballots.

Senator Sullivan, who is endorsed by US President Donald Trump, lashed out at his rival on Election Day.

“My opponent’s campaign is literally focused on misleading Alaskans, lying, and cheating,” the 61-year-old told reporters in Anchorage, Alaska’s most populous city.

“We are witnessing the biggest election cheating scandal in the history of the state of Alaska – maybe one of the biggest in the US Senate’s history.”

Peltola has denied any knowledge of the decoy candidate plot.

“They are running scared. They got nothing,” she said at a campaign event, according to a video posted Tuesday to her X account. She did not mention the scandal in the clip.

Polls show her and the senator essentially tied in a race that may well decide which US political party holds the majority in the Senate.

Should Sullivan lose, it could pave the way for Democrats to place a dramatic check on Trump’s power in Washington.

Last week The New York Times published a detailed account which claimed that Peltola’s campaign helped orchestrate the decoy candidate scheme, which Senator Sullivan said was designed to siphon votes away from the incumbent.

“Unfortunately, the scheme is working,” he said. “Thousands, likely, of Alaskans are going to mistakenly throw away their vote.”

Trump, fuming over the mischief, has sought to preemptively challenge Alaska’s election results. The effort was rejected by a federal judge.

After casting his ballot in Anchorage, Sullivan said he was prepared to accept defeat if that’s what the results show, “once every legal vote is counted and certified.”

But he believed the scandal, and how it has angered voters, could actually work in his favour.

“I think it drives turnout,” he said.

Federal authorities have launched a criminal investigation into the matter.

According to The Washington Post, the US Department of Justice has sent some 20 target letters in connection with the probe, including to a Democratic elections lawyer whose firm is said to represent Peltola.

Sullivan declined to discuss any potential criminal implications.

“I’ll let the lawyers and the prosecutors and the FBI make those determinations,” Sullivan said.

headline: Trump rages at Fox as US midterms voting wraps
description: US president attacks Fox over ratings and a poll as he hosts a White House viewing party, with Democrats favoured to take the House
author: AFP
article_text:
President Donald Trump lashed out at conservative channel Fox News on Tuesday in a sign of early frustration as he watched the US midterm election results at the White House.

The 80-year-old posted three angry messages on his Truth Social network about Fox, blaming its recent ratings decline on not being sufficiently loyal to him.

In one post sent as the first polls closed, Trump said Fox was “way down, not because of me, but because they are AGAINST me!”

In another post, Trump blasted one host as “DUMB AS A ROCK”, and in a third he slammed a Fox poll of voters’ opinions as “always the worst.”

“FoxNews Ratings are way down (27%!) because they’re spending too much time covering the Trump Deranged Dumocrats!” Trump added.

The midterm elections will determine whether Republicans keep control of Congress and will shape the rest of Trump’s second term.

His rageposting came shortly before he hosted an “election night viewing reception” for cabinet members and administration officials in the East Room of the White House.

A White House official had earlier described the mood there as “cautiously optimistic.”

“The president has left it all out on the field, and he’s done everything that was needed. Republicans are in a better spot now than they were four weeks ago,” the official told AFP.

Trump held near-daily rallies in the month before the midterms, urging Republicans to “pretend I’m on the ballot” despite his own record-low approval ratings.

But polls show Democrats with a good chance of seizing the House and possibly the Senate amid voter anger over the economy and the Iran war.

Trump threatened in a telephone interview with the CBS network on Tuesday to be “Mr Veto” and block any Democratic legislation if they win.

headline: Cooper, Warner and Ossoff projected to win Senate races as Democrats make gains
description: Democrats secure a crucial Republican-held seat in North Carolina, while projected victories in Virginia and Georgia boost the party's midterm prospects
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Democrats have secured an early boost in the 2026 US midterm elections, with media projections showing Roy Cooper winning a crucial Senate seat in North Carolina, while Mark Warner and Jon Ossoff have retained their seats in Virginia and Georgia, respectively.

NBC News and ABC News projected Cooper’s victory over Republican Michael Whatley, a former chairman of the Republican National Committee, in North Carolina.

Cooper, the state’s outgoing governor, will replace retiring Republican Senator Thom Tillis, who has emerged as a prominent critic of President Donald Trump.

The victory gives Democrats a crucial pickup in the 100-member Senate as the party seeks to wrest control of Congress from Republicans.

Meanwhile, CNN’s Decision Desk and the Associated Press projected Warner’s victory over Republican candidate Bert Mizusawa in Virginia, securing him a fourth Senate term.

Warner, 71, previously served as Virginia’s governor and was first elected to the Senate in 2008. He is currently the vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee and was among eight US lawmakers briefed on the decision to launch a war against Iran.

In Georgia, NBC News and CBS News projected Democratic Senator Ossoff’s victory over Republican Mike Collins.

Ossoff, who is seen as a potential contender in the 2028 presidential election, retained his Senate seat. His victory does not represent a pickup for Democrats but is nevertheless a positive development for the party.

The early projections offer a boost to Democrats in an election that could reshape the balance of power in Congress and pose a significant challenge to Trump’s administration.

Congress faces battle for control

All 435 seats in the US House of Representatives and 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats are being contested in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Voters in 36 states are also electing governors.

Republicans held narrow majorities in both chambers of Congress before the elections.

The Senate comprises 100 members, with 51 seats required for a simple majority. Before the vote, Republicans held 53 seats, Democrats had 45, while two senators were independents.

The Senate race is expected to be particularly competitive in states where Republicans have traditionally held strong positions, including Kansas, Texas, Iowa, Ohio and Alaska.

Opinion polls have indicated that Democratic candidates are either narrowly ahead or in competitive races against Republican contenders in several of these states.

Election analysis firm Decision Desk HQ has projected that Democrats could win 52 Senate seats, compared with 48 for Republicans.

Democrats eye House majority

The battle for the House of Representatives is also expected to be closely contested.

A party needs 218 seats to secure a majority in the 435-member chamber. Before the elections, Republicans held 218 seats, while Democrats had 212.

Decision Desk HQ has projected a Democratic majority, forecasting 241 seats for the party against 194 for Republicans.

A Democratic takeover of either chamber would significantly affect Trump’s ability to advance his legislative agenda during the second half of his presidency.

The midterm elections are therefore being closely watched as a key test of the president’s political standing and the electorate’s response to his administration.

headline: Democrats flip North Carolina Senate seat as battle for chamber takes shape
description: Democrat Cooper wins Republican-held seat in North Carolina
author: Reuters
article_text:
Democrats won major Senate races in North Carolina and Georgia, but it remained unclear whether the party would succeed in wresting control of the chamber from President ​Donald Trump’s Republicans with millions of votes still uncounted in Tuesday’s midterm elections.

In North Carolina, former Governor Roy Cooper easily defeated Trump-backed Republican Michael Whatley to win a ‌Republican-held seat, media outlets projected, giving Democrats one of the four net pickups they need to win a majority.

Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, widely seen as a potential 2028 presidential candidate, defeated US Representative Mike Collins in Georgia in a contest that was once considered competitive but moved out of reach for Republicans amid Trump’s declining approval ratings.

As of 8:30 p.m. ET (0130 GMT), US media had projected winners in about four dozen House races, though few were among the contests expected ​to be decisive in determining congressional control. Democrats need to net three House seats to take over the chamber.

According to exit polls conducted by SSRS on behalf of a consortium of ​US media outlets including major television networks and the Associated Press, half of voters nationwide said they saw the 2026 midterm elections as an opportunity to ⁠rebuke the president, and three-quarters said they are “angry” or “dissatisfied” with the way the country is headed.

In addition, 70% of voters surveyed said they want Congress to provide more checks and balances on the ​president.

Democrats were favoured to win the House, while the Senate battle was unfolding across several closely contested states, as millions of Americans cast ballots in an election that served as a referendum on the first ​two years of Trump’s second term. Trump himself told his supporters to “pretend I’m on the ballot.”

History is against Republicans: The sitting president’s party has lost ground in Congress in all but two midterms since World War Two. Trump’s approval rating is hovering near his career lows, with voters frustrated by war with Iran, higher fuel prices and wider affordability concerns.

Led by Trump, Republicans have portrayed Democratic candidates as radical, un-American and even communist, labels Democrats flatly reject.

The president has sought to ​energise his base with more than two dozen campaign rallies since the start of October, most in states he easily won in 2024, underscoring Republicans’ defensive posture.

Opinion polls show voters are most concerned about ​affordability and disapprove of Trump’s handling of the issue. His tariffs on imports, many of which the courts threw out, and his decision to attack Iran in February raised prices for consumers.

TRUMP DEPLOYS ELECTION MONITORS

There are 47 US ‌House races widely ⁠seen as competitive, according to a Reuters analysis of the leading election forecasters. If the other contests all proceed as predicted, Democrats would need to win only 13 of those races to secure a majority.

But Democrats have little margin for error in the Senate. The party must defend all of its current seats while winning at least two states that voted for Trump by a double-digit margin two years ago, such as Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas.

Opinion polls show Democrats either narrowly leading or within striking distance in all of those states.

Legal observers and Democrats have warned that Trump, who has long ​falsely claimed that US elections are rigged, may attempt ​to challenge Tuesday’s results if Republicans lose.

The US ⁠Justice Department said it had deployed 1,000 election monitors and observers to all 50 states in what it called the largest Election Day monitoring effort in history.

Democrats criticised the plan as potential voter intimidation. In roughly two-thirds of the jurisdictions the department listed, voters supported Democrat Kamala Harris over Trump in the ​2024 presidential election, a Reuters analysis found.

ELECTION INTRIGUE IN ALASKA

A New York Times report upended the Alaska Senate race when it reported that the ​campaign of Democratic candidate Mary ⁠Peltola, 53, helped recruit a third candidate to run as an independent who shares the first and last name of her Republican opponent, Dan Sullivan, 61.

Peltola has denied involvement. Trump’s Justice Department has launched a criminal probe into the allegations and filed a lawsuit to block certification of the election results, though a judge dismissed the latter effort.

Supporters of the incumbent Sullivan said they were not confused by the presence of two Dan Sullivans on the ballot.

“They ⁠make it pretty ​obvious: It says ‘incumbent’ after his name,” said Jake Wesley, 27, who grew up in Anchorage and is now stationed there ​in the US Air Force. In recent days, Trump has complained repeatedly that voters may not know the meaning of the word.
